title: Doggerland: Lost at Sea
summary: Hosts explore Doggerland, a submerged former land bridge in the North Sea that once connected Britain and continental Europe. They cover its name origin (Dogger Bank, Dutch cod boats), early clues such as Noah's Woods tree stumps and mammal bones in peat (moorlog) hauled up by fishermen, the Reids' 1913 Submerged Forests study, the 1931 Kalinda trawler harpoon find and the Godwins' pollen analysis, Bријany Coles' 1998 Doggerland paper, Vincent Gaffney and Simon Fitch's seafloor mapping project using oil-company survey data, the environmental history from tundra to forest to Mesolithic and Neolithic settlement, Neanderthal and Homo antecessor finds, the causes of submergence (sea level rise, isostatic rebound, possible Storegga tsunamis), and threats from North Sea wind farms. The episode closes with a listener email about Nikola Tesla and radio.

segments.title: Opening banter and what Doggerland is
segments.summary: Hosts introduce Doggerland as a lost, submerged land off Europe in the North Sea that once connected the UK and Europe, and make tangential jokes about the name and a movie.

segments.title: Name origin and the North Sea
segments.summary: The name comes from the Dogger Bank, a shallow productive fishing area named after Dutch cod boats. The North Sea is a shallow, long-used shipping and trade route, and oil and gas reservoirs were found there in the 1950s and 1960s.

segments.title: Noah's Woods and moorlog peat
segments.summary: Fishermen dragging up moorlog peat found mammal bones from the nineteenth century onward. Medieval locals saw tree stumps at low tide, called Noah's Woods. H. G. Wells wrote a story speculating about a continent under the North Sea.
topics: H. G. Wells Story of the Stone Age

segments.title: Reids and Submerged Forests
segments.summary: Clement and Eleanor Reid studied the tree stumps and peat and in 1913 published Submerged Forests, the first study on the woods. They concluded sea level rise had sunk the land.

segments.title: 1931 Kalinda harpoon and Godwins' pollen analysis
segments.summary: In 1931 the trawler Kalinda, skippered by Pilgrim Lockwood, pulled up a carved antler harpoon head. The British Museum declined it. Harry and Margaret Godwin used pollen analysis showing freshwater wetland peat, proving humans were on land above the sea.

segments.title: Dating finds and early human remains
segments.summary: The harpoon head is dated to about 14,000 years old, early Mesolithic. Other twentieth-century finds include textile bits and a Neanderthal skull fragment of 70,000 to 40,000 years old, with a facial reconstruction.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Hosts take a break before returning to the topic.

segments.title: Briony Coles names Doggerland
segments.summary: In 1998 archaeologist Briony Coles published Doggerland: A Speculative Survey, coining the name after the Dogger Bank and proposing people lived on a land bridge. She built maps from fishermen's anecdotes showing the land at different periods.

segments.title: Gaffney and Fitch seafloor mapping
segments.summary: Vincent Gaffney and graduate student Simon Fitch obtained seafloor survey data for 23,000 square kilometers from Petroleum Geo Services, an oil company, and mapped Doggerland, showing it was a substantial populated region. Archaeology Magazine called it the largest geophysical survey made available to archaeologists.

segments.title: Gaffney's later work and underwater archaeology
segments.summary: Gaffney founded the Submerged Landscape Research Group at Bradford in 2014 and joined the Unpathed Waters project in 2022. Underwater archaeology techniques like suction excavation are discussed, and the Unpathed Waters maps are recommended.

segments.title: Fishermen, sediment, and the vegetation timeline
segments.summary: Fishermen now share GPS data for finds, though sediment from rivers makes sites hard to find. Vegetation changed from tundra in the Younger Dryas to birch and pine forest, then hazel woods and freshwater lakes.

segments.title: Animals, Homo antecessor, Neanderthals and Homo sapiens
segments.summary: Ice age megafauna like woolly rhinoceros and mammoths died out or moved north, replaced by wild boar, otters and beavers. Homo antecessor was there about 800,000 years ago. A Neanderthal skull fragment from off the Netherlands coast, dated to about 70,000 years, was named Kranj. Homo sapiens arrived around 14,000 years ago as hunter-gatherers.

segments.title: Neolithic farming and Bouldnor Cliff
segments.summary: Doggerland's warmer climate allowed farming, marking the start of the Neolithic transition. Bouldnor Cliff off the Isle of Wight has a possible dock, burials, houses and pits.

segments.title: Why Doggerland sank: sea level, isostatic rebound, tsunamis
segments.summary: Sea levels rose as glaciers melted, and Doggerland sank as the land had been raised by glacial weight. The Storegga slides in the Norwegian Sea may have caused tsunamis about 8,000 years ago that reached 25 miles inland; Gaffney doubted they wiped out the land. Doggerland was fully submerged roughly 5,000 to 7,000 years ago.

segments.title: Wind farms threat to Doggerland sites
segments.summary: Shallow North Sea sites are attractive for bolted-on wind turbines, which threaten archaeological sites and ecology.

segments.title: Listener email on Tesla and My Sharona
segments.summary: A listener named Andy praises Chuck's guitar solo taste and argues Nikola Tesla deserves more credit as the father of radio over Marconi. Hosts suggest a future Tesla episode.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts sign off and give the email address and podcast credit.
